draft.title: Symbolism in literature
card: A symbol is an object, colour or setting that stands for an idea. A dove can stand for peace, and a red rose can stand for love.
A symbol is still a real thing in the story. A dove is a bird on the page, and it also points to an idea beyond itself.
A symbol can gather meaning across a text. If a writer keeps returning to the same object, each appearance can add to what it stands for.
To read a symbol, ask what the thing is, where it appears, and what idea it seems to point to. Look for clues in the text that support your reading.
draft.remember: A symbol is a thing that stands for an idea, and its meaning can grow each time it returns.

a.q: In a story, a locked gate appears at the start, middle and end of Ravi's life in a small town, and he feels trapped each time. What is the gate most likely to be?
opts: A symbol of being trapped
A symbol of freedom
A plain object with no meaning
A comparison using the word like
a.why: The gate keeps returning and Ravi feels trapped each time, so it gathers the meaning of being trapped. It is not freedom, because the clues in the story point the other way.
a.clue: What does Ravi feel each time the gate appears?

b.q: In a novel, Lena's grandmother's old teapot is mentioned when the family argues, when they move house and when they finally reunite. Each time it is kept safe. What does this repeated use best show about the teapot?
opts: It gathers meaning as a symbol of family bonds
It stands for an idea only the first time it appears
It is a symbol only because it is an old object
It is not a symbol because it is a real teapot
b.why: The teapot returns during major family events and is always kept safe, so it gathers the meaning of family bonds. It can be a real teapot and a symbol at once, so being a real object does not rule it out.
b.clue: A symbol can still be a real thing in the story.

b.best: It gathers meaning as a symbol of family bonds

problems.detail: The stem says Ravi 'feels trapped each time', and the right option repeats the word 'trapped'. A student can match the words without understanding symbolism. The clue points to the same word, which makes the giveaway stronger.

Two distractors use 'only' ('only the first time', 'only because it is an old object'), which marks them as overstatements. The right option is also the only one with a precise idea ('family bonds'), so it stands out from the others.

a.q: Ravi dreams of moving to the city. At the start, middle and end of the story, he stands at a locked gate on the edge of his small town. What idea does the gate most likely stand for?
opts: Being held back from the life he wants
The freedom to choose his own path
His pride in the town he grew up in
His joy at starting a new journey
a.why: Ravi wants a life beyond the town, and the gate between him and the road out is locked each time he stands there. So it points to being held back. Freedom is the opposite, because a locked gate stops him from going where he wants.
a.clue: Think about what Ravi wants and what a locked gate does.

b.q: In a novel, Lena's grandmother's old teapot appears when the family argues, when they move house and when they finally reunite. Each time it is kept safe. What does the teapot most likely come to stand for?
opts: A family bond that lasts through every change
The arguments that keep dividing the family
The family's wish to throw out the past
The family's wealth and costly belongings
b.why: The teapot returns at each major family event, including the reunion, and is always kept safe, so it gathers the meaning of a bond that survives change. The arguments are tempting, but they are only one of the scenes, and the teapot is protected through all of them.
b.clue: Look at every scene it appears in, not just one.

a.best: Being held back from the life he wants

b.best: A family bond that lasts through every change
